young.html: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel was a German professor who lived about 200 years ago. He asked a big question: what does it really mean to be free?

Many people say freedom means doing whatever you want. Hegel thought that was only the beginning. Think of a game of soccer. Without rules, there is no game at all, just a crowd kicking a ball. The rules do not take away the players' freedom; they make the game possible. Hegel thought families, schools, jobs and laws can work the same way: good ones help people become who they want to be.

young.name: gb-hegel-right
young.cap: Hegel's book climbs in five steps, from owning things to living in a free country. Tap each step.

young.html: Rules that make things possible. List three games or activities you like. For each, name one rule. Then ask: would the game be more fun, or less, without that rule? Which rules make you more free?

full.html: G. W. F. Hegel (1770–1831) grew up in Stuttgart, studied theology at Tübingen with the poet Hölderlin and the philosopher Schelling, and taught at Jena, Nuremberg and Heidelberg before he became professor of philosophy at Berlin in 1818. He was nineteen when the French Revolution began, and he spent his life thinking about what it had promised: a world built on freedom. The Philosophy of Right (1820, dated 1821) was his textbook for his Berlin lectures on law, ethics and the state.

By right (German Recht) Hegel means much more than law. He means every way that freedom becomes real in the world: owning things, keeping promises, acting on conscience, family life, work and trade, and citizenship.

full.name: gb-hegel-right
full.cap: Our summary of the book's three parts, with ethical life divided into its three forms.

full.html: The book climbs in three parts. Abstract right is freedom at its thinnest: I am a person, I can own property, I can make contracts. Morality turns inward, to intention and conscience. Ethical life brings the two together in shared institutions: the family, civil society and the state.

full.text: Its mandate is: Be a person and respect others as persons.
full.author: Hegel
full.work: Philosophy of Right, section 36 (on abstract right)

full.html: Hegel's big claim is that freedom is not only something inside a person. It needs a world to live in: customs, laws and institutions that free people can recognize as their own. He calls this ethical life (Sittlichkeit).

Hegel was one of the first philosophers to give the modern economy its own place in a theory of the state. He had read Adam Smith and the other economists. In civil society each person pursues his own interest, and yet everyone depends on everyone else, like threads in a web. Hegel admired this world of work and trade, and he also saw its dangers: he wrote that great wealth and great poverty grow side by side, and that a society can leave some people with no stake in it. He hoped courts, public authorities and trade associations would hold it together.

At the top stands the state, a constitutional monarchy with a written law, an educated civil service and an assembly of estates. For Hegel the state is not just a contract people sign to protect their property; it is the place where citizens come to see the common good as their own good too.

Hegel's praise of the state is the most argued-over part of the book. Some critics, especially in the 20th century, read it as worship of state power. Many scholars answer that Hegel defended the rule of law, property, conscience and a constitution, and attacked rulers who stand above the law. Both readings start from real passages in the book, so it is worth reading it yourself.
The Preface ends with one of the most famous images in philosophy. Philosophy, Hegel says, does not tell the world what it ought to be; it comes along afterward and understands it.

full.text: When philosophy paints its grey in grey, one form of life has become old, and by means of grey it cannot be rejuvenated, but only known. The owl of Minerva takes its flight only when the shades of night are gathering.
full.author: Hegel
full.note: Minerva is the Roman goddess of wisdom; the owl was her bird.

full.html: The same Preface contains another famous line, in Dyde's words: "What is rational is real; And what is real is rational." Some readers took it as approval of whatever exists. Hegel later explained that by "real" he meant what truly lives up to its own nature, not everything that happens to be around.
Thinking Hegel's "right" means only courtroom law. In this book a loving family and an honest day's work are forms of right too.

deep.html: Hegel's students split after his death. "Right" Hegelians stressed his respect for existing institutions and religion; "Left" or "Young" Hegelians, among them Karl Marx, used his ideas to criticize the society of their day. Marx's first major manuscript was a critique of this very book. Later, liberal critics such as Karl Popper (1945) accused Hegel of paving the way for the all-powerful state; scholars such as Shlomo Avineri and Allen Wood replied that this misreads a defender of modern constitutional government. The debate continues.

deep.text: Hegel and earlier books on this ladder

items: Plato's Republic and Aristotle's Politics: Hegel admired the Greek city, where citizens felt at one with their laws, but thought it left no room for individual conscience.
Locke and Rousseau: Hegel rejected the idea that the state is a contract among individuals, but kept Rousseau's idea of a general will in a new form.
Kant: Hegel's "morality" is his answer to Kant. He praised Kant's idea of duty but thought duty alone is empty without a world of customs and institutions.
Adam Smith: Hegel's civil society takes over Smith's picture of a market linking strangers.
Is freedom doing what you want, or being able to become who you want to be?
Can rules and institutions make people more free? When do they make them less free?
Does a person owe anything to the community that raised them?
Can philosophy only understand the world, or can it change it? (Marx, later on this ladder, gave a famous answer.)

deep.html: Hegel's other rung here, The Philosophy of History, tells the story of how, in his view, freedom came into the world.

questions: What rules at home or school make you more free? Do any make you less free?
Hegel thought love, not a contract, holds a family together. What do you think holds your family together?
Is it fair that some people get rich while others stay poor in a market? What could a community do about it?
What does it mean to see the common good as your own good?
The owl of Minerva flies at dusk. Can you think of something you understood only after it was over?
